pros: Captures global importance: nodes that bridge different parts of the network
More informative than degree for identifying critical connectors
Identifies bottlenecks whose removal would fragment the network
Brandes' algorithm is asymptotically optimal for exact computation
Theoretically well-founded with clear mathematical definition
Applicable to both directed and undirected graphs
Works with weighted edges (e.g., road distances, communication costs)
Each source node computation is independent (parallelizable)
Can be approximated via sampling for very large graphs
cons: Computationally expensive: O(V·(V+E)) limits to graphs with < 10⁵ nodes
Requires all-pairs shortest paths — memory and time intensive
Impractical for real-time analysis of large dynamic networks
Assumes flows always follow shortest paths (may not hold in practice)
Nodes in different components receive zero centrality
Sensitive to graph structure changes (non-robust to edge insertion/deletion)
Normalization between directed and undirected graphs differs
Cannot distinguish between different types of shortest paths
Result interpretation can be non-intuitive for complex networks
High memory overhead for storing all predecessor lists simultaneously
Does not account for alternative paths (all shortest paths weighted equally)
